opus-5.5.text:
I think generality in a robot brain is often misunderstood. When people hear "general," they imagine one model that can do everything—fold laundry, cook, assemble furniture—right out of the box. But to me, generality is less about the number of tasks you can list and more about whether the system has learned something transferable about the physical world.

Let me put it this way. A specialized robot learns a mapping: in this scene, with these objects, do this motion. A general robot brain should learn the underlying structure—how objects respond when you push them, what "graspable" means across thousands of shapes, how a goal described in language connects to a sequence of physical changes. If you've truly learned that structure, then a new task isn't really new. It's a recombination of things you already understand.

So I'd break generality into a few layers. The first is perceptual generality: can you see and understand an unfamiliar environment—a different kitchen, different lighting, objects you've never seen? The second is embodiment generality: can the same brain drive different bodies, a two-arm robot, a mobile base, maybe a humanoid, with only modest adaptation? And the third, which I think is the hardest, is task or behavioral generality: given an instruction you've never been trained on, can you figure out a reasonable way to accomplish it?

Language models gave us a strong intuition here. People didn't train GPT on every possible question; generality emerged from scale and from data that captured the structure of human knowledge. Many of us hope the same will happen in robotics. But the difference is that the physical world doesn't come pre-tokenized on the internet. Robot interaction data is scarce, expensive, and highly tied to specific hardware. That's why I think the path to generality has to lean heavily on things like world models and video data—learning how the world evolves from massive amounts of observation, then grounding that knowledge with a smaller amount of real action data.

And one more point: I don't think generality and reliability are opposites, but in practice there's a tension. A general model that succeeds 70% of the time on everything is impressive in a demo but not useful in a home or factory. So for me, real generality means the model can quickly reach high reliability in a new setting—with a few demonstrations, or a bit of self-practice. Generality isn't the finish line; it's the foundation that makes specialization cheap.

r001.rationale: The response says a general brain should work across different robot bodies, but it does not state that a robot’s embodiment determines which usage scenarios suit it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that "generality" in a robot brain is often misunderstood as "one model that can do everything." That's not really how I think about it. To me, generality is about the ability to transfer: when you encounter a new task, a new object, a new environment, or even a new robot body, how much of what you already know can you reuse, and how little new data do you need to adapt?

If you look at how humans work, we don't learn to pour water from a kettle and then start from zero when we switch to a teapot. We have a world model, we have a sense of physics, we understand intention, and the specific motion is almost the last detail. A lot of today's robot learning is the opposite: the motion is learned first, very specifically, and the understanding is thin. So the model looks impressive on the task it was trained on and collapses once anything shifts.

So when I think about generality, I break it into a few layers. The first is perception and understanding, which is where vision and language models have already made huge progress. A robot brain should understand a scene the way a large multimodal model does, not just detect boxes. The second layer is reasoning about tasks: decomposing a goal into steps, knowing what to do when something fails, understanding that if the cup is upside down you flip it before pouring. That's closer to what language models are good at. The third layer, and the hardest one, is action: actually producing the low-level control that works on a real body with real physics, real friction, real delays.

The reason this is hard is that the data distribution for action is completely different from text or images. The internet gave us trillions of tokens for language and billions of images, but there's no internet of robot actions. So the real question of generality is: how do you let the first two layers, which can benefit from internet-scale data, carry the third one? How do you make the action layer small, adaptable, and grounded, instead of trying to brute-force it with data you don't have?

My own view is that generality will come from a combination. One part is a strong foundation model that handles understanding and planning, trained on video, language, and simulation, because video especially contains a lot of implicit knowledge about how the world moves. Another part is an action model that is relatively body-agnostic, learned from a mix of teleoperation, simulation, and human video, with the ability to be fine-tuned quickly on a new embodiment. And the glue is a shared representation, something like a common language between what the robot sees, what it wants to achieve, and what it does with its arms.

I also want to emphasize that generality is not binary. A model that works on fifty tasks across three kinds of kitchens is already a form of generality, even if it's not AGI for robots. I'm a bit skeptical of the framing that we'll have one giant model and suddenly robots can do anything. I think it will look more like a gradient: the scope of transfer keeps widening, the amount of task-specific data keeps shrinking, and at some point it crosses a threshold where deploying to a new scenario feels more like configuring than like training. That's the moment when it becomes economically meaningful, and that's what I'm actually working toward.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transfer to a new robot body and body-agnostic action models, but does not state that a robot’s embodiment determines which usage scenarios it is suited to.

astra-6.text:
I think generality in a robot brain means that you don’t have to build a new brain for every new task. The robot can reuse what it has learned when the object, the environment, or the instruction changes.

For example, if a robot learns to pick up a cup, can it pick up a cup it hasn’t seen before? Can it do that in a different kitchen? And can it use that ability as part of a longer task, like clearing a table? Those are different levels of generality.

There’s also the question of transferring across robot bodies. The underlying understanding of a task may be shared, but the way you execute it depends on your sensors, your arms, and your hands. So I wouldn’t equate a general robot brain with exactly the same behavior on every robot.

For me, the key test is what happens outside the training setup: how much carries over, how much new experience is needed, and whether the robot can recognize a mistake and recover. Generality isn’t just the number of tasks you can demonstrate. It’s the ability to adapt when things change.

r001.rationale: The response says sensors, arms, and hands affect how a task is executed across robot bodies, but does not state that embodiment partly determines which usage scenarios a robot is suited to.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generality in a robot brain means being able to handle changes without having to learn everything from scratch. If a robot learns to pick up a cup, can it pick up a different cup, in a different room, with different lighting? And can it use what it learned to do a related task, like putting that cup into a dishwasher?

There are several dimensions here: different tasks, different environments, and even different robot bodies. A system might be very capable across tasks on one robot but struggle when the camera position or the gripper changes. So generality is a matter of degree, and we should be specific about which changes a system can handle.

For me, the key is whether the robot can reuse its experience, adapt with a small amount of new information, and recognize when it doesn’t know enough to act reliably. That’s a more meaningful measure than simply counting how many demonstrations or tasks it has seen.

r001.rationale: The response says generality can vary across robot bodies and that camera or gripper changes may cause difficulty, but it does not state that a robot’s embodiment determines which usage scenarios it is suited to.
